sections.h2: Assessor and Collector offices in Hernando
sections.html:
DeSoto County property tax involves two desks at the same Hernando address. In Suite 100 of 365 Losher Street the Tax Assessor (662-469-8029) puts a value on every parcel. In Suite 110 the Tax Collector (662-469-8030) issues the bill and receives payment. A second collection counter operates on BJ Chain Drive in Olive Branch, handy if you live in the north end.

Mississippi requires a new valuation of real property at least every four years and of taxable personal property annually. The assessor does not have to go inside your home. Rates are not on a ballot for you. Each of the county, your city and the school district decides how much money it needs, and local officials combine that into the millage that lands on your statement.

Mississippi property classes and assessment ratios
ClassWhat it coversAssessment ratio
Class ISingle-family, owner-occupied home10%
Class IIOther real property, such as rentals and land15%
Class IIIBusiness personal property15%
Class IVPublic utility property30%
Class VMotor vehicles30%

Multiply true value by the class ratio, then by millage, and you have the tax. Because a rented house falls in Class II, a larger fraction of its value is taxed than for a home its owner lives in.

Whoever holds title on January 1 is the person assessed. Statements show up in November and December, with February 1 as the payment date. Should that date fall on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, paying on the Monday after carries no penalty or interest.

Real estate left unpaid can be offered at the county tax sale. The calendar differs by county, with some picking the first Monday in April and others the last Monday in August. Phone the collector to learn which applies in DeSoto.

  • A winning bidder at that sale gets no instant clean title, since the former owner keeps two years from the sale to redeem (Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3).
  • With no bidder, the parcel goes to the State of Mississippi, and the Secretary of State handles it at 1-866-835-2637.
  • Unpaid tax clouds the title, so a title company will want it cleared when you close.

Your route runs through the Chancery Clerk, who arranges a hearing in front of the county Board of Supervisors. Put the request in by the first Monday in August, which lands ahead of the tax due date.

Before you file, talk to the assessor and carry comparable sales or repair bids. A cracked foundation or an aging roof is far easier to prove with photographs and a contractor's quote than with argument. The board checks valuations, listens to objections and then adopts the rolls, so the August date does not bend.

Homestead trims the bill for the person living in the house, and it stays with that owner rather than the property. The window to apply at the Tax Assessor is January 1 through April 1. Unless ownership or marital status changes, the filing carries forward and you skip the yearly paperwork.

For an owner who is 65 or older, or totally disabled and otherwise eligible, the first $75,000 of true value is exempt from tax. Two things block it: the owner or spouse being out of compliance with state income tax laws, and a vehicle tagged outside the home county. Buyers who intend to live in the house should apply in their first year, because after April 1 the benefit waits for the next assessment year.

A tax balance seldom blocks a sale. Your title company gets the payoff from the collector and deducts it before handing you your check. When the parcel was already sold at a tax sale, the redemption sum is deducted as well.

Watch for these local snags:

  • Confirm that the name, mailing address and homestead status on the roll are current. A statement mailed to an old address is still owed.
  • An inherited house may carry unpaid tax or paperwork never recorded, and both must be fixed before the deed can move.
  • A tenant-occupied rental sits in Class II, with the higher ratio, which an investor buyer will notice.
  • A newer subdivision may be inside a city levy while a house outside the limits is not, so similar homes can see different bills.

Selling for cash trims some of that, since the buyer takes the house as is and the closing date is yours to pick. The title still has to be clean, any mortgage paid off and the current year's tax settled on the closing statement.

sections.h2: A quick way to find your balance
sections.html:
Use the county's online tax search first. It lets you look up real and personal property by name, parcel or address and shows what is due. A phone call to the collector then catches items that print separately, such as tax-sale and earlier-year amounts.

  1. Pull the parcel number off your deed or the assessor's lookup.
  2. Ask the Tax Collector, in Hernando or Olive Branch, for the current and earlier-year figures.
  3. Check with the Chancery Clerk to see whether a sale was ever held on the parcel.
  4. Pass every number to the title company so it can settle taxes at closing.

Treat this page as general background, not legal or tax advice, and verify each date and amount with the county before relying on it.

The county occupies the far northwest of Mississippi, just south of Shelby County, Tennessee, with Hernando as seat. Four cities hold most residents: Hernando, Horn Lake, Olive Branch and Southaven. Walls is a town, and places such as Lake View, Lynchburg and Pleasant Hill are census-designated. Lake Cormorant, Nesbit and Cockrum are unincorporated.

Your parcel's tax district settles whether a city or school levy applies, so check that before pricing a sale. The 2020 census counted 185,314 people, and the 2025 estimate is 197,918. One school system, the DeSoto County School District, covers everyone, and the largest in the state, although attendance zones vary by address.

The county farmed cotton first, then dairy and soybeans, before subdivisions replaced the fields. Homes in Southaven went on sale in 1958, and Interstate 55 opened through Hernando in 1964. The population was 67,910 in 1990 and reached 161,252 by 2010. Houses here span several building eras: a 1970s ranch in Horn Lake and a 2010s two-story in Olive Branch face different repair lists, even though the same collector bills both.

Interstate 55, Interstate 69, Interstate 269, U.S. 51 and U.S. 61 carry most traffic. The county has no fixed-route transit of its own, so most households depend on a car.

faqs.q: When are DeSoto County property taxes due?
faqs.a: February 1, covering property assessed the year before. If that day is a weekend or holiday, the following Monday still counts with no penalty.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in DeSoto County?
faqs.a: Bring it to the Tax Collector at 365 Losher Street, Suite 110, Hernando, or the Olive Branch branch. The Hernando number is 662-469-8030, and it is smart to confirm hours and payment types first.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my DeSoto County assessment?
faqs.a: Ask the Chancery Clerk to put you before the Board of Supervisors. File by the first Monday in August, before the tax comes due.

faqs.q: Can I sell a DeSoto County house with taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes, and it happens often. The title company collects the payoff figure and pays the county from your sale proceeds. A parcel sold at a tax sale also has to have its redemption amount paid.

faqs.q: Does DeSoto County have one school district?
faqs.a: Yes, a single countywide district, and it is the largest in Mississippi. Ask the district which attendance zone covers a specific address.
